What Is White Label IoT?

White label IoT refers to pre-built connected devices or platforms developed by one company and rebranded by another. These solutions come ready for market, allowing companies to deploy IoT capabilities without having to design and manufacture the hardware or software from the ground up.

White-Label IoT Monitoring for MSPs and Resellers
Reselling under your own brand gets a new revenue line live in weeks. Building your own platform takes years.
Why build your own IoT platform when you can resell one
Inside the Hydra reseller program: branding, provisioning, revenue share

NetNeural's Hydra reseller program is built around three things a reseller actually needs to sell IoT monitoring under their own name: a branded customer experience, a provisioning workflow that doesn't require reseller engineering time, and a revenue share structure that makes the economics work.

On branding, the dashboard, alerts, and reports a reseller's customers see carry the reseller's own name and identity, not NetNeural's. A customer signing up through a reseller shouldn't need to know NetNeural exists at all unless the reseller chooses to disclose it.

On provisioning, new customer accounts and sensor deployments go through a workflow built for a reseller managing many end customers, not a single-tenant setup process repeated manually for each one. Hardware ships, gets placed, and reports into the right customer's branded environment without the reseller needing to build any of that infrastructure themselves.
On revenue share, the rate is set by deployed sensor volume rather than negotiated case by case. Every reseller starts at 10% off list and moves up a published ladder as their deployed base grows:
(250-1,499) earns 15%, plus a 1% performance bonus and a 2% override on sub-resellers.

The commercial model underneath a reseller agreement is per-sensor, per-month. There is no base platform fee on a paid plan and no seat licence to buy before the first sensor reports - a reseller's cost scales with what they actually have deployed and billing, which means a pilot of five sensors costs roughly a fiftieth of a rollout of two hundred and fifty rather than carrying a minimum.

The reseller discount applies to that per-sensor rate, so margin is the gap between the discounted rate a reseller pays and whatever they choose to charge their own customer. NetNeural does not set or see the reseller's end-customer price - the reseller owns the commercial relationship, including what the monitoring is worth to that account.

For deployments with no existing connectivity, a cellular gateway is available as hardware, and the LoRaWAN path covers sites where running a sensor network over kilometres is cheaper than putting a SIM in every device. Those are options, not requirements - a reseller bringing their own connectivity is the expected case, not an exception the platform tolerates.

There's no fixed countdown - ramp time depends on how quickly a reseller has pilot customers ready to deploy to, not a calendar. What is fixed is the process: once an application is approved, a new reseller's dashboard opens with a guided walkthrough covering payouts, downline (recruiting sub-resellers), invites, and support, so the mechanics of the program are covered from day one.

From there, the shape of a reseller's early rollout is: get the branded portal configured and tested, run an initial deployment with one or two pilot customers to validate the provisioning workflow end to end, then scale to a broader customer base once that pilot deployment is working smoothly.

Reselling allows OEMs to offer connected services with relatively little development effort. The technology is already available, and deployment can be comparatively fast.
